title: Chemistry: All 118 Elements
description: For beginning chemistry learners: all 118 symbols, names, atomic numbers, groups or inner-transition series, and one fact each. Lanthanoids and actinoids use series labels to avoid disputed group-3 placement.

sources.name: Original educational explanations from general subject knowledge

cards.back: Hydrogen. Atomic number: 1. Group 1. The lightest element; its most common isotope has no neutron.
Helium. Atomic number: 2. Group 18. It was detected in the Sun's spectrum before it was identified on Earth.
Lithium. Atomic number: 3. Group 1. It is the lightest metal.
Beryllium. Atomic number: 4. Group 2. It occurs in the mineral beryl.
Boron. Atomic number: 5. Group 13. Boron compounds are used in borosilicate glass.
Carbon. Atomic number: 6. Group 14. Diamond and graphite are different structural forms of this element.
Nitrogen. Atomic number: 7. Group 15. Diatomic nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of dry air by volume.
Oxygen. Atomic number: 8. Group 16. Diatomic oxygen makes up about 21 percent of dry air by volume.
Fluorine. Atomic number: 9. Group 17. It has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale.
Neon. Atomic number: 10. Group 18. An electrical discharge through neon produces a reddish-orange glow.
Sodium. Atomic number: 11. Group 1. Its symbol comes from the Latin name natrium.
Magnesium. Atomic number: 12. Group 2. A magnesium ion sits at the center of the chlorophyll ring.
Aluminium. Atomic number: 13. Group 13. It is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust; aluminum is the US spelling.
Silicon. Atomic number: 14. Group 14. It is widely used as a semiconductor in electronic chips.
Phosphorus. Atomic number: 15. Group 15. Phosphate groups are components of DNA and ATP.
Sulfur. Atomic number: 16. Group 16. Elemental sulfur commonly forms yellow solids.
Chlorine. Atomic number: 17. Group 17. Chloride ions are one component of table salt.
Argon. Atomic number: 18. Group 18. It is the most abundant noble gas in Earth's atmosphere.
Potassium. Atomic number: 19. Group 1. Its symbol comes from kalium.
Calcium. Atomic number: 20. Group 2. Calcium phosphate minerals are major components of bones and teeth.
Scandium. Atomic number: 21. Group 3. Its name refers to Scandinavia.
Titanium. Atomic number: 22. Group 4. A protective oxide layer contributes to its corrosion resistance.
Vanadium. Atomic number: 23. Group 5. It is added to some steels to improve their properties.
Chromium. Atomic number: 24. Group 6. Chromium helps stainless steel resist corrosion.
Manganese. Atomic number: 25. Group 7. Manganese dioxide is used in some common dry-cell batteries.
Iron. Atomic number: 26. Group 8. It is the main metallic component of steel.
Cobalt. Atomic number: 27. Group 9. A cobalt atom is part of vitamin B12.
Nickel. Atomic number: 28. Group 10. It is used in many corrosion-resistant alloys.
Copper. Atomic number: 29. Group 11. It has high electrical conductivity and is used in wiring.
Zinc. Atomic number: 30. Group 12. Zinc coatings protect steel by galvanization.
Gallium. Atomic number: 31. Group 13. It melts near 30 degrees Celsius, just above typical room temperature.
Germanium. Atomic number: 32. Group 14. It is a semiconductor used in some electronic and optical devices.
Arsenic. Atomic number: 33. Group 15. Gallium arsenide is a compound semiconductor.
Selenium. Atomic number: 34. Group 16. Its name derives from the Greek word for the Moon.
Bromine. Atomic number: 35. Group 17. It is a liquid nonmetal at ordinary room temperature.
Krypton. Atomic number: 36. Group 18. Its name derives from a Greek word meaning hidden.
Rubidium. Atomic number: 37. Group 1. Its name refers to deep-red lines in its emission spectrum.
Strontium. Atomic number: 38. Group 2. Strontium compounds can produce red colors in fireworks.
Yttrium. Atomic number: 39. Group 3. Its name comes from the Swedish village of Ytterby.
Zirconium. Atomic number: 40. Group 4. Zirconium alloys are used as cladding for nuclear fuel.
Niobium. Atomic number: 41. Group 5. Niobium-titanium alloys are used in superconducting magnets.
Molybdenum. Atomic number: 42. Group 6. It is used in alloys designed to withstand high temperatures.
Technetium. Atomic number: 43. Group 7. It has no stable isotopes.
Ruthenium. Atomic number: 44. Group 8. It is one of the platinum-group metals.
Rhodium. Atomic number: 45. Group 9. It is used in catalytic converters.
Palladium. Atomic number: 46. Group 10. It can absorb substantial quantities of hydrogen.
Silver. Atomic number: 47. Group 11. Pure silver has the highest electrical conductivity among metals near room temperature.
Cadmium. Atomic number: 48. Group 12. It has been used in nickel-cadmium rechargeable batteries.
Indium. Atomic number: 49. Group 13. Indium tin oxide is used as a transparent conducting material.
Tin. Atomic number: 50. Group 14. Its symbol comes from the Latin stannum.
Antimony. Atomic number: 51. Group 15. Its symbol comes from stibium.
Tellurium. Atomic number: 52. Group 16. Its name derives from a Latin word for Earth.
Iodine. Atomic number: 53. Group 17. Iodine is a constituent of thyroid hormones.
Xenon. Atomic number: 54. Group 18. It forms chemical compounds, including xenon fluorides.
Caesium. Atomic number: 55. Group 1. A transition in caesium-133 defines the SI second; cesium is the US spelling.
Barium. Atomic number: 56. Group 2. Barium compounds can give fireworks green colors.
Lanthanum. Atomic number: 57. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Its name derives from a Greek word meaning to lie hidden.
Cerium. Atomic number: 58. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres.

Praseodymium. Atomic number: 59. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Its name refers to a green twin, reflecting the history of its separation.
Neodymium. Atomic number: 60. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It is used in strong neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnets.
Promethium. Atomic number: 61. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It has no stable isotopes.
Samarium. Atomic number: 62. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Samarium-cobalt alloys are used in permanent magnets.
Europium. Atomic number: 63. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Europium compounds are used in red-emitting phosphors.

Gadolinium. Atomic number: 64. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Natural gadolinium has a large capacity to absorb thermal neutrons.
Terbium. Atomic number: 65. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Terbium compounds are used in green-emitting phosphors.

Dysprosium. Atomic number: 66. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It can help permanent magnets retain performance at higher temperatures.
Holmium. Atomic number: 67. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Its name comes from Holmia, a Latin name for Stockholm.

Erbium. Atomic number: 68. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Erbium-doped optical fibers amplify signals in telecommunications.

Thulium. Atomic number: 69. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Its name refers to Thule, an ancient name associated with the far north.
Ytterbium. Atomic number: 70. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It is one of several elements named after Ytterby.
Lutetium. Atomic number: 71. Lanthanoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Its name comes from Lutetia, the ancient name for Paris.
Hafnium. Atomic number: 72. Group 4. Its name comes from Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen.
Tantalum. Atomic number: 73. Group 5. It is used in compact electronic capacitors.
Tungsten. Atomic number: 74. Group 6. Its symbol comes from wolfram.
Rhenium. Atomic number: 75. Group 7. Its name refers to the Rhine River.
Osmium. Atomic number: 76. Group 8. It is among the densest elements under ordinary conditions.
Iridium. Atomic number: 77. Group 9. It is highly resistant to corrosion.
Platinum. Atomic number: 78. Group 10. It is widely used as a catalyst.
Gold. Atomic number: 79. Group 11. Its symbol comes from the Latin aurum.
Mercury. Atomic number: 80. Group 12. It is a liquid metal at ordinary room temperature.
Thallium. Atomic number: 81. Group 13. Its name refers to a green shoot, inspired by a green spectral line.
Lead. Atomic number: 82. Group 14. Its symbol comes from the Latin plumbum.
Bismuth. Atomic number: 83. Group 15. Bismuth-209 is radioactive but has an extraordinarily long half-life.
Polonium. Atomic number: 84. Group 16. Marie Curie named it after Poland.
Astatine. Atomic number: 85. Group 17. All of its known isotopes are radioactive.
Radon. Atomic number: 86. Group 18. It is a radioactive noble gas formed in natural decay chains.
Francium. Atomic number: 87. Group 1. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey.
Radium. Atomic number: 88. Group 2. It occurs naturally as a product in radioactive decay chains.
Actinium. Atomic number: 89. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Its name derives from a Greek word for ray.
Thorium. Atomic number: 90. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named after Thor, the Norse god.

Protactinium. Atomic number: 91. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Its name reflects its relationship to actinium in a decay chain.

Uranium. Atomic number: 92. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Uranium-235 can sustain a fission chain reaction under suitable conditions.
Neptunium. Atomic number: 93. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named after Neptune.
Plutonium. Atomic number: 94. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named after Pluto.
Americium. Atomic number: 95. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Americium-241 is used in some ionization smoke detectors.
Curium. Atomic number: 96. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named in honor of Marie and Pierre Curie.
Berkelium. Atomic number: 97. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named after Berkeley, California.
Californium. Atomic number: 98. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. Californium-252 is used as a neutron source.
Einsteinium. Atomic number: 99. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named in honor of Albert Einstein.
Fermium. Atomic number: 100. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named in honor of Enrico Fermi.
Mendelevium. Atomic number: 101. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named in honor of Dmitri Mendeleev.
Nobelium. Atomic number: 102. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named in honor of Alfred Nobel.
Lawrencium. Atomic number: 103. Actinoid series; no single numbered group is assigned here because group-3 placement conventions differ. It was named in honor of Ernest Lawrence.
Rutherfordium. Atomic number: 104. Group 4. It was named in honor of Ernest Rutherford.
Dubnium. Atomic number: 105. Group 5. It was named after Dubna, Russia.
Seaborgium. Atomic number: 106. Group 6. It was named in honor of Glenn Seaborg.
Bohrium. Atomic number: 107. Group 7. It was named in honor of Niels Bohr.
Hassium. Atomic number: 108. Group 8. Its name refers to the German state of Hesse.
Meitnerium. Atomic number: 109. Group 9. It was named in honor of Lise Meitner.
Darmstadtium. Atomic number: 110. Group 10. It was named after Darmstadt, Germany.
Roentgenium. Atomic number: 111. Group 11. It was named in honor of Wilhelm Röntgen.
Copernicium. Atomic number: 112. Group 12. It was named in honor of Nicolaus Copernicus.
Nihonium. Atomic number: 113. Group 13. Its name derives from Nihon, a Japanese name for Japan.
Flerovium. Atomic number: 114. Group 14. It was named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions.
Moscovium. Atomic number: 115. Group 15. It was named after the Moscow region.
Livermorium. Atomic number: 116. Group 16. It was named after Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.
Tennessine. Atomic number: 117. Group 17. It was named after Tennessee.
Oganesson. Atomic number: 118. Group 18. It was named in honor of Yuri Oganessian; bulk properties are not established from macroscopic samples.
